newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin defends decision to stop Gestapo museum.
newsitem.headline: Berlin defends decision to stop Gestapo museum.

text.p: Germany's Jewish community attacked the city of Berlin on Thursday for halting work on a museum on the site of the former Gestapo secret police.
But Klaus Landowsky, head of the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) in the city parliament, hit back at critics. There was, he said, no money for the 45 million mark ($30 million) project.
"I do not need to be taught history lessons about World War Two and Germany's coming to terms with its history," Landowsky said during a debate in city parliament.
"We have to cut costs. We will look for ways to build the museum together with the federal government after the year 2000."
About 30 demonstrators gathered to protest against the decision on Thursday on the empty, windswept lot where Hitler's Gestapo security police and SS headquarters once stood.

Nazi leaders such as Heinrich Himmler and Adolf Eichmann had their offices in the buildings, which served both as an interrogation centre for enemies of the regime and headquarters for a vast system of repression that culminated in the concentration camps.
"This decision is extremely regrettable," said Ignatz Bubis, head of the Central Council of Jews in Germany.
"I can understand the city needs to save money," he said in an interview with SFB radio. "But what will happen in 2000? Will there be more money? Or will it be pushed back again?"

City mayor Eberhard Diepgen had led a widely publicised groundbreaking ceremony for the project on May 8, 1995, the same day world leaders were in Berlin for ceremonies marking the 50th anniversary of the end of World War Two.

Unfurling a huge black banner that read "Put off for 50 years and now blocked by the Senate", the demonstrators said they were outraged the city was spending hundreds of millions of marks (dollars) on sport facilities but could not find the money for the Gestapo museum.

"It is a disgrace that Berlin still does not have a central memorial to the Gestapo terror," said Andreas Nachama, the museum's director. "This is a great loss for the city and its international image."
Wolfgang Wieland, the leader of Berlin's Greens party, added: "The city is more interested in spending money on prestige buildings than on coming to terms with its history."

The buildings were heavily damaged during the war and the ruins were cleared in the early post-war years. The lot served as a dump and later a go-cart track in the no-man's land just west of where the Berlin Wall that divided the city stood.
After the Wall fell, several temporary signs describing the Gestapo terror and how it was organised in the buildings on the site were put up on the lot.
In 1995 after decades of false starts and delays, the city and federal governments announced plans to share the cost of a permanent museum and documentation centre.
"It is an outrage that this project is now being postponed, probably forever," said Wieland.
